attempts.raw_response: The studio said it would use the information to understand the scale of the problem and potentially take action against repeat offenders. Miles Jacobson, the studio director, explained that the data showed illegal downloads were happening across dozens of countries, with some regions accounting for disproportionately high numbers. He argued that piracy was not a victimless crime, pointing out that lost revenue could have been invested in improving the game and hiring new staff. The company previously introduced an unusual anti-piracy measure, embedding code that caused in-game injuries to skyrocket for those playing pirated copies. Despite these efforts, Jacobson admitted that fully eliminating piracy remained unrealistic, though he hoped greater awareness would encourage more players to purchase legitimate copies.

pair.human_continuation: "We've worked out that that's 8.5 million individuals," said Mr Jacobson. "Around 1.4 million of those people have logged into the game more than five times, so those are people that are playing the game quite a lot." The survey of Tiga members suggested a minority were in favour of punishing people using pirated games. Of those asked, 73% said they disagreed with slowing or cutting the internet connection of those who swapped copyrighted files. "UK developers are taking the initiative to deal with the issue of piracy and are looking for new ways of delivering content and communicating directly with their consumers," said Dr Wilson. "This is testament to the generally pragmatic and innovative approach of the UK video game industry."
